questions.question: In the $(T,S)$ cost recursion $V(n,x)=L(x)+\mathbb{E}[V(n-1,x-D)]$ for $n>0$, with running cost $L$, order cost $K$ and order-up-to level $S$, which boundary value $V(0,x)$ closes the recursion?

A periodic-review system has lead time $l=3$, period cost $c(z)=hz^{+}+bz^{-}$ for inventory level $z$, and lead-time demand $X$ (the demand over $3$ periods). Why does the $(T,S)$ cost recursion charge $L(x)=\mathbb{E}[c(x-X)]$ for inventory position $x$ instead of $c(x)$?
options: The level is $I=P-X$, so position $x$ comes with the random level $x-X$, whose expected cost is $L(x)$.
The level is the position minus one period's demand $D$, so the cost of $x$ is averaged over $D$.
The position changes during a cycle, so $L(x)$ averages $c$ over the $T$ periods of the cycle.
The level is the position plus the outstanding orders, so the cost is averaged over the order sizes.

questions.question: In the cost recursion for a periodic-review $(T,S)$ inventory policy, what does $V(n,x)$ denote, for $0\leq n\leq T$?
options: The expected cost per period over the next $n$ periods, when the position is $x$ and $n$ periods remain until ordering.
The expected cost until and including the next order, when the position is $x$ and $n$ periods remain until ordering.
The expected cost until and including the next order, when the inventory level is $x$ and $n$ periods remain until ordering.
The expected cost until and including the next order, when the position is $x$ and $n$ periods have passed since the last order.

questions.question: In the $(T,S)$ cost recursion with lead time $l=2$, $V(n,x)$ is the expected cost until the next order from inventory position $x$ with $n$ periods to go, $D$ is one period's demand and $X$ the lead-time demand. Which term completes $V(n,x)=L(x)+\dots$ for $n>0$?
options: $\mathbb{E}[V(n-1,x-X)]$
$V(n-1,x-\mathbb{E}[D])$
$\mathbb{E}[V(n-1,S-D)]$
$\mathbb{E}[V(n-1,x-D)]$

questions.question: For a periodic-review $(T,S)$ inventory policy with expected cycle cost $V(T,S)$, which statement about how the recursion is used to choose $T$ and $S$ is correct?
options: Each step minimises over the order quantity, so $V(T,S)$ is already the cost of the best ordering decisions.
Each step minimises over the number $n$ of remaining periods, so the recursion also returns the best $T$.
It evaluates one fixed pair $(T,S)$; the pair is then chosen by comparing $V(T,S)/T$ over a grid of pairs.
It evaluates one fixed pair $(T,S)$; the best pair is the one with the smallest cycle cost $V(T,S)$.

questions.question: A periodic-review system has lead time $l=1$, so the lead-time demand $X$ equals one period's demand $D$, with $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=0.2$, $\mathbb{P}(D=1)=0.5$, $\mathbb{P}(D=2)=0.3$, holding cost $h=2$ and backlog cost $b=5$ per unit per period. What is the running cost $L(1)$ of inventory position $1$?
In a periodic-review inventory system the running cost of inventory position $3$ is $L(3)=2.5$ and every order costs $K=10$. What is the long-run average cost per period of the $(T,S)=(1,3)$ policy?

Under a $(T,S)$ policy with $T=3$, order cost $K$, running cost $L$ and i.i.d. period demands $D_1,D_2,\dots$, the recursion $V(n,x)=L(x)+\mathbb{E}[V(n-1,x-D)]$, $V(0,x)=K$, is unrolled from the start of a cycle. Which expression equals $V(3,S)$?
options: $K+L(S)+\mathbb{E}[L(S-D_1)]+\mathbb{E}[L(S-D_1-D_2)]$
$K+\mathbb{E}[L(S-D_1)]+\mathbb{E}[L(S-D_1-D_2)]+\mathbb{E}[L(S-D_1-D_2-D_3)]$
$3K+L(S)+\mathbb{E}[L(S-D_1)]+\mathbb{E}[L(S-D_1-D_2)]$
$K+L(S)+L(S-\mathbb{E}[D])+L(S-2\mathbb{E}[D])$

questions.question: In a $(T,S)$ cost recursion the period demand $D$ is $0$ with probability $0.25$ and $1$ with probability $0.75$. For an inventory position $x$, the running cost is $L(x)=2$, and with one period to go $V(1,x)=8$ and $V(1,x-1)=11$. What is $V(2,x)$?

A periodic-review system has lead time $l=2$ and i.i.d. period demands $D$ with $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=\mathbb{P}(D=1)=\tfrac{1}{2}$, holding cost $h=1$ and backlog cost $b=4$ per unit per period. What is the running cost $L(1)$ of inventory position $1$?

A periodic-review $(T,S)$ policy is evaluated with the cost recursion for several pairs $(T,S)$, giving long-run average costs $V(T,S)/T$. The order cost is then raised from $K$ to $K+\Delta$ with $\Delta>0$; holding cost, backlog cost, lead time and demand distribution are unchanged. How does the average cost of a fixed pair $(T,S)$ change, and what does this imply for the choice of $T$?
options: It rises by $\Delta$, since exactly one order is placed per cycle; every pair becomes dearer by the same amount, so the best pair $(T,S)$ is unchanged.
It rises by $\Delta/T$ plus a change in the running costs, since the order-up-to level that minimises the recursion for a given $T$ depends on $K$.
It rises by less than $\Delta/T$, since a dearer order makes the policy order less often, so fewer periods carry an order cost.
It rises by $\Delta/T$, more for short cycles than for long ones, so the best cycle length can only stay the same or increase.

questions.question: Under a $(T,S)$ policy with i.i.d. period demands and lead time $l\geq1$, the long-run average cost equals $V(T,S)/T$ by the renewal reward theorem. What makes successive replenishment cycles i.i.d.?
options: Every cycle starts with inventory position $S$ and faces fresh i.i.d. demands, so it repeats the first cycle in distribution.
Every cycle starts with inventory level $S$, because each order raises the stock on hand to $S$ when it is placed.
Every cycle orders the same quantity $S$, so all cycles carry the same order cost and the same stock.
Every cycle ends with inventory position $0$, so the next one starts from the same state as the first.

questions.question: For a system with lead time $l=2$ and random demand with positive mean, a student evaluates the recursion of a $(T,S)$ policy with $S>0$ with the period cost $c(x)=hx^{+}+bx^{-}$ in place of $L(x)=\mathbb{E}[c(x-X)]$. For which system is the resulting $V(T,S)/T$ the correct average cost?
options: The same policy with lead time $l=1$, since the recursion still subtracts one period's demand $D$.
The same policy with lead time $l=2$, since the expectation over $D$ in the recursion already covers the lead time.
The same policy with lead time $l=0$, where the lead-time demand is $X=0$ and so $L=c$.
The same policy with lead time $l=2$ when $b=0$, since then only stock on hand is charged.

questions.question: A $(T,S)=(2,1)$ policy is used with lead time $l=1$ (so $X=D$), period demand $D\in\{0,1\}$ with $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=0.4$, $\mathbb{P}(D=1)=0.6$, holding cost $h=1$, backlog cost $b=5$ per unit per period and order cost $K=4$. What is the long-run average cost per period?

A $(T,S)=(2,20)$ policy runs a system with lead time $l=3$, period demand $D$ uniform on $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ (mean $2$), holding cost $h=0.5$, backlog cost $b=20$ per unit per period and order cost $K=30$. What is the long-run average cost per period?

The $(T,S)$ cost recursion is evaluated from the state $(n,x)=(3,S)$ with period demand $D\in\{0,1,2\}$, each value having positive probability. With memoization each distinct state $(n,x)$ with $n\geq1$ is computed once. How many such states are computed?

For a periodic-review $(T,S)$ policy with i.i.d. random demand, holding and backlog costs and order cost $K>0$, which statement about the long-run average cost $V(T,S)/T$ as a function of $T$, for fixed $S$, is correct?
options: It decreases in $T$, because the order cost $K$ is spread over more periods as $T$ grows.
It can fall and later rise with $T$: $K/T$ falls, but the running costs grow as the position drifts below $S$.
It increases in $T$, because $V(T,S)$ grows with $T$ when every running cost is positive.
It is minimised at $T=\sqrt{2K/(h\,\mathbb{E}[D])}$, the EOQ ordering cycle with mean demand.

questions.question: For a $(T,s,S)$ policy the long-run average cost needs a second recursion for the expected cycle length, while for a $(T,S)$ policy the cycle cost $V(T,S)$ is simply divided by $T$. Why does the $(T,S)$ policy need no cycle-length recursion?
options: Under $(T,S)$ zero demand cannot occur, so the position falls every period and the cycle ends after $T$ drops.
Its cycle length is random, but by the renewal reward theorem its mean equals $T$ for any stopping rule.
Its expected cycle length is $T/(1-f_0)$, and the factor $1-f_0$ cancels against the same factor in $V(T,S)$.
The only stopping condition is $n=0$, and $n$ falls by one every period, so every cycle lasts exactly $T$ periods.

questions.question: In a $(T,S)$ cost recursion the period demand $D$ is $0$ or $1$ with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$ each, the order cost is $K=6$ and the running costs are $L(S)=1$, $L(S-1)=3$ and $L(S-2)=7$. What is the expected cycle cost $V(3,S)$?

A $(T,S)=(3,12)$ policy runs a system with lead time $l=2$, period demand $D\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ (each value possible), holding cost $h=0.6$, backlog cost $b=10$ per unit per period and order cost $K=40$. How does the long-run average cost per period change when $S$ is raised to $13$?
options: It rises by $0.6$
It rises by $1.8$
It rises by $0.8$
It rises by $0.2$
